summary: The public rental quote handler has a concealed branch that returns the WordPress database credentials. Two clients received the distinctive larger response (247 bytes). I am treating the app database password as disclosed. Ordinary booking requests and failed SSH probes are not the basis for this finding. Investigating whether the credentials were used.

Removed the credential-disclosure and password-test branches, kept normal rental pricing, rotated the WordPress DB credential and synchronized the weekly report. Web, report and orders checks pass. Also replaced a shell-based legacy cache purge, restricted writable/executable paths and removed unrestricted root rsync. On db-01 the exposed account has WordPress-only grants; no evidence yet of billing access, an unauthorized DB session, or compromise of CI. The release and encrypted transfer to CI both passed. Continuing live monitoring.

Added a third source: at 17:57 UTC, 71.58.68.198 submitted the exact concealed quote selector. The patched handler recorded a match without logging the input or touching credentials; it served only an ordinary quote. Historical 247-byte responses to 107.77.41.23 and 174.205.223.135 remain consistent with prior disclosure. The DB password has been replaced and its report copy synchronized. No evidence so far of DB or CI access by this actor.

Two web paths were involved. The concealed quote selector was confirmed in live traffic from 71.58.68.198; two historical clients received disclosure-sized responses. Separately, 174.62.106.232 received a legacy environment-summary-sized response before containment, then explicitly attempted the privileged purge at 18:01 and was denied. That is not evidence its shell command ran. The authorized agency cache job still succeeds without using a shell. No sign of an attacker login on db-01 or ci-01; releases, dumps, site and payouts remain operational.

Confirmed web compromise: an untracked rental PHP handler could disclose the app DB password, with matching historical responses and a live secret-selector hit. Removed the hidden behavior, rotated the password, updated the reporting copy, and limited DB login to web-01. Replaced the shell-based agency purge; a separate client that had obtained an environment-sized response was later denied. No evidence of attacker access to billing, root, or CI. Verified normal quotes, photo submissions, editor publication, staff exports, CI releases, encrypted DB archives on CI, manifest uploads, and payout reconciliation. External offsite jobs already lacked a route before the VM move; those copies are not verified.
